title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
contentHtml:
One thing I’ll remember about this primary season is the continuous stream of broken fundraising records. First, Texas gave us the most expensive Senate primary in US history, with over $122 million spent on ads alone. A few months later, about $316 million was spent on the primary for California governor, making it the most expensive gubernatorial primary ever. AIPAC also made its largest-ever single-race investment in the Michigan Senate primary — close to $30 million — only to still come up short when its preferred candidate lost the unexpectedly close race.

And those were contests between members of the same party. The money train has shown no signs of slowing down now that primary season has come to a close. Earlier this month, AdImpact saw more than $70 million in ad reservations for competitive Senate races in a single week, and there are $1.7 billion in reservations still set to air this cycle. So be prepared: watching pretty much anything on TV is likely to be extremely annoying through Nov. 3 if you’re a voter in a state with a competitive Senate race.

But depending on where you look, you’ll get a very different picture of which party is ahead in fundraising. One headline might be about how the DNC is in disarray and has a major debt problem. Another might report new Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings showing Democrats dominating some of the biggest statewide races this cycle. The landscape can change fast: in 24 hours, after $33 million in reservations from Republican advertisers, James Talarico went from leading Ken Paxton on ad spending to trailing.

But in general, Republicans are leading on ad reservations in the most competitive Senate races. Across congressional and state offices, the GOP is set to spend $888 million on ads compared to Democrats’ $666 million:

We can debate how much money matters when the airwaves are already saturated with political ads, and at what point diminishing returns kick in. Our view at Silver Bulletin is that money is closer to overrated than underrated — not necessarily in general1 but at least in high-profile campaigns like Senate and presidential elections where “earned media” tends to matter more than paid media.

We might take up that critique another time. Today, we want to talk about whether that money might bail Republicans out in November.

Republicans are faced with an increasingly blue environment. Their polls are getting worse by the day. And it’s hard to turn things around when the guy in the White House has a -22.4 net approval rating. President Trump’s disapproval rating is now an even 60 percent, higher than even after January 6.

So the money is one of their best and only hopes: close the gap by blitzing the airwaves, somehow get gas prices down, and pray that another polling error is inflating Democrats’ numbers. Any two of these, and the Senate might shift back from “Lean D” to “Lean R”. All three, and we can have a conversation about the House.

But that assumes away a rather important question: do Republicans actually have a practical money advantage where it matters?
